## The questions

Three things a prospective user of a parallel CFD solver actually wants to know, each answered here
by measurement:

1. **Does weak scaling survive the interconnect?** On-node parallelism is cheap; the test of a
   distributed incompressible solver is what happens to its global pressure solve when halo
   exchanges and reductions start crossing nodes.
2. **What does the same code deliver on CPU and on GPU**, from a workstation to a national
   supercomputer (Snellius: Genoa nodes with 192 cores; H100 nodes with 4 GPUs)?
3. **How does it compare with leading open-source codes** on the identical case? We run three
   references, chosen to bracket the design space:
   - [**CaNS**](https://github.com/CaNS-World/CaNS) — the state of the art in raw speed for
     *trivial geometry*: explicit RK3 + an exact FFT Poisson solve, possible only on boxes.
   - [**incflo**](https://github.com/AMReX-Fluids/incflo) — the DOE-exascale (AMReX) solver in
     peclet's *own method family*: finite-volume incompressible NS, geometric-multigrid
     projections, embedded-boundary capable.
   - **OpenFOAM** (ESI v2412) — the ubiquitous general-purpose unstructured code, `icoFoam` + GAMG.

## The instrument: a boundary-free Taylor–Green box

Scaling studies want a case that grows without complications. We tile a triply periodic box with
**Taylor–Green vortices** (one vortex per $64^3$ tile, $\mathrm{Re}_\text{tile}=100$): no walls,
every cell does identical work, and the domain extends in any direction by adding tiles. The TGV
initial condition is also a Stokes eigenfunction, giving the driver a built-in analytic
correctness check (matched to $2\times10^{-3}$, identical across rank counts and backends).

[`tgv_bench.py`](tgv_bench.py) runs the case distributed and reports warmup-excluded per-step wall
time with a per-phase breakdown (predictor / momentum solve / pressure projection), the pressure
iteration count, and the accumulated time and count of every global reduction inside the pressure
solve — so algorithmic effects and communication effects are never conflated.

**Fairness rules, applied symmetrically.** Every code runs the identical grids at matched
per-step tolerances (pressure ~1e-5/1e-6 class; CaNS's FFT solve is exact); timings are
steady-state per-step wall times, excluding each code's setup (meshing, FFT plans, grid
initialization). References run *expert-tuned*, not default: incflo gets `max_grid_size=64` and
MLMG tolerances matched to the study (its AMReX defaults — $32^3$ box shredding and ~1e-11
tolerances — cost it a measured 1.53×, which we refuse to charge it). OpenFOAM uses GAMG with a
64-bit-label build (required above ~2×10⁸ cells). CaNS runs its recommended adaptive CFL 0.95 —
its RK3 step advances ~4× more physical time per step than the fixed-CFL codes, which per-step
throughput comparisons deliberately do not penalize. On the cluster, single measurements are
noise: production points are pinned (`--cpu-bind=cores`) and taken as the **median of three
draws** (bound draws reproduce to ±5 %; the figures show every draw).

## Workstation (24-core Threadripper PRO 5965WX, RTX 5080)

### Hybrid MPI × OpenMP mix

![Left: throughput by MPI ranks × OpenMP threads on 24 cores (fixed $192^3$ TGV). Right: the
per-phase step decomposition.](workstation_mix.png)

**12 ranks × 2 threads is the sweet spot (11.8 Mcell/s)** — vs 9.8 for pure MPI and a 14× speedup
over serial. The phase split shows why: the momentum and pressure sweeps are memory-bandwidth
bound, so what matters is feeding all memory channels without paying 24 ranks' worth of halo
surface and per-rank multigrid boilerplate. The same shape reappears on Genoa (below): some MPI is
good, all-MPI is not.

### Weak scaling within one node: four codes, one wall

![Weak scaling at 2.1 M cells/rank, pure MPI, up to 24 cores. Left: efficiency vs. own 1-rank
baseline. Right: absolute throughput (log scale); the dotted line is the single RTX 5080 running
the same case.](workstation_weak.png)

With per-rank work fixed, all four codes decay together — and this is not communication (peclet's
pressure iteration count is pinned at 7.0 at every rank count). A single node's weak scaling
measures **shared memory-bandwidth saturation**, nothing else: the efficiency ordering (incflo
43 %, peclet 40 %, CaNS 31 %, OpenFOAM 29 % at 24 ranks) is the *inverse* of per-core bandwidth
demand. Absolute throughput on 24 cores: **CaNS 41 Mcell/s, peclet 9.8, incflo 4.4, OpenFOAM
3.3** — peclet is 3× OpenFOAM and 2.2× incflo at identical settings, while CaNS's 4× lead is the
price of generality made visible: an exact FFT solve that exists *only because* the box is
trivial, against machinery that handles arbitrary cut-cell geometry at large d$t$. **And the
single RTX 5080 at 67 Mcell/s outruns CaNS's entire 24-core node by 1.6×** — the design point of
the suite: the CPU path is a capable oracle, the GPU path is the product.

### Single-GPU ladder (RTX 5080, 16 GB): three codes on the same device

Both GPU-capable references run here from the same sources as their CPU curves: incflo via its
AMReX CUDA backend, CaNS via its OpenACC + cuDecomp backend (NVIDIA HPC SDK toolchain, cuFFT).
OpenFOAM has no native GPU solver path. All three at their GPU-fair settings.

| grid | cells | peclet | incflo | CaNS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $128^3$ | 2.1 M | 67.4 | 16.1 | **131.6** |
| $160^3$ | 4.1 M | 60.7 | 17.9 | **136.8** |
| $192^3$ | 7.1 M | 67.2 | 18.6 | **138.3** |
| $208^3$ | 9.0 M | 34.0 | 18.7 | **129.7** |

*(Mcell/s, higher is better.)* Two clean results:

- **peclet is 3.6× incflo on the same GPU** — a wider margin than on CPU (2.2×), the GPU-first
  design paying off where it is meant to.
- **CaNS leads peclet 2× on a single device** — with no communication to pay, the exact FFT solve
  sets the throughput ceiling, and this is the honest price tag of general geometry. Notably the
  gap *narrows* from 4× on CPU to 2× on GPU. What happens to that lead once the FFT's all-to-all
  meets the interconnect is the multi-GPU question — on CPU it inverted before two nodes.

peclet holds ~60–67 Mcell/s until 16 GB fills; the $208^3$ dip is *algorithmic*, not hardware —
208 supports only a $13^3$-bottomed multigrid whose odd coarse level weakens the preconditioner.
Grids with generous power-of-two content keep the hierarchy deep — a practical sizing rule.

## Does the domain decomposition care about awkward rank counts?

Sweeping prime and composite rank counts on a fixed $192^3$ box (pure MPI, 5965WX):

| ranks | ms/step | Mcell/s | pressure iters | max-block imbalance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 2634 | 2.7 | 8.0 | 1.04× |
| 7 (prime) | 2015 | 3.5 | 8.0 | 1.02× |
| **8** | 1579 | 4.5 | **6.9** | 1.00× |
| 13 (prime) | 1186 | 6.0 | 7.9 | 1.08× |
| **16** | 945 | 7.5 | **7.2** | 1.00× |
| 23 (prime) | 819 | 8.6 | 8.0 | 1.20× |

**Barely.** Non-power-of-two counts pay one extra pressure iteration (the ORB's uneven subtree
splits land off the deepest multigrid coarsening grid, trimming the bottom level) and at worst a
20 % max-block imbalance — throughput sits on the same trend line as the neighbouring powers of
two. Users can pick rank counts by hardware, not by numerology.

## Cross-node CPU weak scaling on Snellius Genoa

The central experiment: 188.7 M cells *per node* (768×640×384 each), grown with the node count on
Genoa (192 cores/node), every code on the identical case. peclet runs its measured single-node
optimum (96 ranks × 2 threads — 59 Mcell/s on one node, 6× the whole workstation); the references
run their natural pure-MPI mode.

![Cross-node weak scaling on Snellius Genoa, 188.7 Mcells/node fixed. Left: efficiency vs own
1-node baseline (open circles: individual peclet draws). Right: aggregate throughput; the dotted
line is ideal scaling at peclet's slope.](snellius_weak.png)

| nodes | peclet (median) | CaNS | incflo | OpenFOAM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 45 Mcell/s — 100 % | **109 — 100 %** | 16 — 100 % | 9.4 — 100 % |
| 2 | 86 — 96 % | 20 — 9 % | 32 — 99 % | — |
| 4 | 167 — 93 % | 153 — 35 % | 67 — 103 % | — |
| 8 | **266 — 74 %** | 45 — **5 %** | 117 — 90 % | — |

Three structural results:

1. **The two geometric-multigrid codes scale; the FFT code does not.** peclet (96/93/74 %) and
   incflo (99/103/90 %, single draws) both hold near-flat cross-node curves — halo exchanges plus
   a handful of latency-bound reductions per iteration survive the interconnect. peclet's
   instrumentation makes the cost precise: iterations pinned at 8.1, global-reduction time growing
   like the expected log-term to ~9 % of the step at 8 nodes.
2. **CaNS's single-node crown does not survive the interconnect.** 2.4× faster than peclet on one
   node — and by two nodes it has collapsed to 9 % efficiency (reproduced in independent runs), at
   eight nodes to 5 %: **eight CaNS nodes deliver the throughput of one peclet node.** Its FFT
   solve requires global all-to-all transposes every substep — nearly free in shared memory,
   ruinous across nodes. (Caveat: CaNS ran its automatic pencil-grid choice; expert `dims` tuning
   may soften, but cannot remove, the all-to-all.) **The crossover lands before two nodes**: any
   problem too big for one node is already a problem where peclet outruns the FFT state of the art.
3. **Within the method family, peclet leads on speed at equal scaling**: ~2.8× incflo per node
   with the same flat curve, and 4.8× OpenFOAM on its single-node point. (OpenFOAM's multi-node
   points are limited by its serial mesh generation at these sizes — an operational cost of the
   unstructured design that the structured codes don't have.)

## Multi-GPU weak scaling: 1–32 H100

The same case at 47.2 M cells per GPU (4 H100 per node), 1 → 32 GPUs — from one device to eight
nodes:

![Left: GPU weak scaling, 47.2 Mcells/GPU fixed — 90 % efficiency and 3.5 Gcell/s aggregate at 32
H100s. Right: the pressure-solver ablation at the inter-node points (8 and 16
GPUs).](snellius_gpu.png)

**Weak efficiency stays above 90 % all the way to 32 GPUs** (100 → 94 → 93 → 92 → 92 → 90 %), with
iterations pinned at 12.2 and the entire global-reduction budget at 6.5 ms of a 426 ms step
(1.5 %) at 32 GPUs. In absolute terms: **one H100 delivers 123 Mcell/s — 2.7 Genoa nodes'
worth — and 32 H100s sustain 3.5 Gcell/s**, a grid of 1.5 billion cells advancing more than two
time steps per second.

The ablation on the right is how the solver's defaults are chosen — measured, at scale:

- **MG-PCG with fine-scoped nullspace removal** (the default) wins outright: the pressure solve
  performs ~5 all-reduces per Krylov iteration, few enough that even across 8 nodes the reduction
  tax stays negligible.
- Removing the mean on every multigrid level instead ("all") costs 5.5 % — pure reduction latency.
- The host-staged halo costs 12 % vs GPU-aware MPI (device pointers straight to the interconnect).
- **Chebyshev**, the classical reduction-free alternative, loses 2.6×: it needs 38 iterations
  against PCG's 12, and at ~5 reductions/iteration PCG's information advantage beats Chebyshev's
  communication advantage everywhere we can measure.
- An agglomerated algebraic bottom solve (GraphAMG) buys fewer iterations (7.4) but pays far more
  than it saves at these scales.

## What the study says, in one paragraph

On the identical boundary-free case, `peclet.flow` is the fastest general-geometry incompressible
solver in the comparison on every platform tested — 3× OpenFOAM and 2.2× incflo per CPU node, 4.8×
OpenFOAM on Genoa — and the *only* code family in the field (shared with incflo) whose weak
scaling survives the interconnect, holding ~90 % across nodes where the FFT state of the art
collapses below 10 %. The same source runs 67 Mcell/s on a consumer RTX 5080 (outrunning CaNS's
whole 24-core node, 3.6× incflo on the identical GPU, and within 2× of CaNS's own GPU
backend — the FFT ceiling that no general-geometry solver can cross), 123 Mcell/s on one H100,
and 3.5 Gcell/s at 90 % weak efficiency on 32 H100s.
The pressure solve that makes general geometry possible — cut-cell geometric multigrid inside
PCG — costs a measured ~4× against an FFT direct solve on one node, and wins it back with interest
the moment the problem spans two.

## Reproducing

All drivers, case definitions, runner scripts for the three reference codes, the Snellius job
pack, raw result JSONs and the figure scripts live in
[`benchmarks/parallel-scaling/`](https://github.com/computational-chemical-engineering/peclet-examples/tree/main/benchmarks/parallel-scaling)
— `tgv_bench.py` (peclet), `run_cans.sh`, `run_incflo.sh`, `openfoam-tgv/`, `snellius/README.md`
(exact submission commands), `plot_workstation.py` / `plot_snellius.py`.
